name: Paul Graham

education.notes: Switched away from philosophy in spirit late in undergrad after deciding it was 'isolated from the rest of intellectual life'. Programmed in his spare time throughout — first IBM 1401 then a TRS-80 at home as a teenager.
Entered Harvard for AI under Tom Cheatham. Realised AI as practised in the early 80s ('expert systems' in Lisp) was a dead end — pivoted to using Lisp itself as the subject.
PhD thesis on extending Lisp (later published as 'On Lisp').

Started RISD in fall 1992 after a stint at the Accademia di Belle Arti in Florence. Dropped out in 1993 because the BFA foundation programme didn't actually teach painting (his own words in 'What I Worked On').

Confirmed in 'What I Worked On': accepted via entrance exam, started fall 1989, returned to US at the end of the first year. Overlapped with his Harvard PhD which he finished in June 1990 (5-week dissertation sprint on continuations). Canonical example of his 'wide 20s compound' thesis.

keyDecisions: Studied philosophy first, not CS — built a first-principles thinking habit before going technical, then realised philosophy was hollow and bailed.
Switched to AI/CS for grad school but quickly identified that 80s-era symbolic AI was a dead end — pivoted his thesis to Lisp itself, not AI built on Lisp.
Refused to specialise narrowly inside Harvard CS — stayed broad enough to still consider art school.
lessons: Width before depth in your 20s compounds — a liberal-arts foundation sharpens the kind of thinking pure technical training doesn't.
If your field has a dead end at its core (80s AI), don't follow the herd off it — change the subject of your own work.
Notice when you've outgrown the official curriculum.
careerSteps.notes: Programmed since teens (IBM 1401 in junior high, then TRS-80). Always technically capable; the philosophy degree was the unusual choice, not the code.

careerSteps.company: Accademia di Belle Arti, Florence; RISD; freelance
keyDecisions: Took years to study painting after the PhD — explicit choice to broaden rather than monetise early.
Quit RISD when it stopped teaching — refused to stay in a credential for its own sake.
Wrote 'On Lisp' in parallel — kept compounding the technical asset while exploring.
lessons: Painting (and writing) trains 'how to see' — the perceptual habit that later let him spot good founders.
Credentials are tools, not identities — exit them when they stop teaching.
careerSteps.notes: This phase looks like wasted time on a CV but is the load-bearing one for the rest of the arc — gave him the writer/observer identity that powered the essays and YC.

keyDecisions: Stayed independent and broke rather than joining a big company — preserved optionality on his time.
Spotted the commercial web in 1995 — the precise moment Netscape made browser-as-runtime viable.
lessons: The pre-founding 'wandering' phase is often where the founding idea actually germinates.
Being technically deep AND between jobs at the moment a new platform appears is how you become the first mover on it.
careerSteps.notes: Built deep Lisp and early-web technical chops; broke enough that the move to start Viaweb was partly economic.

keyDecisions: Founded at 31, not in his early 20s — disproved his own later trope before he wrote it.
Bet the company on the browser as runtime — 'web app' was barely a concept in 1995; building one for non-technical merchants was a contrarian wager on what HTTP could do.
Wrote Viaweb in Common Lisp despite industry norm being C/C++/Perl — bet on technical leverage (macros, fast iteration) over hireability.
Co-founded with Robert Morris and Trevor Blackwell — Harvard CS relationships, high trust from day one, no co-founder search needed.
Took the Yahoo! acquisition at peak dot-com stock value rather than holding out — converted paper to real wealth at the right moment.
lessons: First-mover on a new platform compounds — Viaweb was effectively the first online store builder of its kind.
Founding age does not have to be 19–22; technical depth and the right wave matter more than youth.
Choose tools for leverage, not for the hiring market — small teams with sharp tools beat large teams with conventional ones.
Sell at the top of the cycle when offered; ego-holding for a higher number is how founders end up with zero.
careerSteps.notes: Started summer 1995 (first working web-app prototype on Aug 12, 1995 per 'What I Worked On'). Acquired by Yahoo! in summer 1998 for ~$49M in Yahoo stock; became Yahoo! Store. PG documented the entire Lisp-as-secret-weapon argument in 'Beating the Averages'.

keyDecisions: Served short post-acquisition tenure, then left — refused to become a long-term employee of his own acquirer.
lessons: Founders rarely thrive long inside acquirers; cash in the lock-up and leave.
An exit is a release, not a new job.

careerSteps.role: Essayist, Hacker News builder, language designer
keyDecisions: Started publishing essays at paulgraham.com — built personal brand and audience before founding YC.
Wrote 'Hackers & Painters' (2004), which became founder-canon reading and pre-loaded the YC brand with credibility.
Designed Arc, a new Lisp dialect — kept doing technical work even after the exit, refusing to drift into pundit-only mode.
Lived off Viaweb money rather than chasing a second startup immediately — bought himself six years of unscheduled thinking.
lessons: Writing publicly builds a network passively. By the time YC launched, PG had a built-in audience of exactly the right people.
Six years 'between things' is not wasted if you're producing thought work that compounds.
Wealth converts into time better than into more wealth.
careerSteps.notes: Essays went viral in spring 2001 when a Lisp talk hit 30,000 page views in a day via Slashdot — the moment the public audience formed. This is the load-bearing period — the essays and the book created the conditions for YC to launch into a ready audience.

keyDecisions: Founded YC with Jessica Livingston (later wife), Robert Morris, and Trevor Blackwell — re-used the Viaweb trust pair plus added Jessica's people-judgement.
Invented the batch-style seed accelerator model — cohort + standard terms + intense mentorship + Demo Day, when seed investing was bespoke and slow.
Wrote 'How to Start a Startup' and other essays that doubled as YC's top-of-funnel marketing — turned the essay habit into a deal-flow machine.
Funded teams, not ideas — let founders pivot freely, which made YC robust to any single thesis being wrong.
lessons: Find a model others haven't tried. Pre-YC, seed investing was bespoke; YC standardised it.
Density of founders beats density of capital. YC's edge is the network among founders, not cheque size.
Distribution can be free if you've already built the audience — YC's marketing was essays PG was going to write anyway.
Bet on people, not theses — it's the only way to be antifragile to your own being wrong about markets.
careerSteps.notes: Founded March 2005 (per 'What I Worked On', born from a conversation at the corner of Garden and Walker streets in Cambridge). Stepped back from active president role in 2014, handed to Sam Altman.

keyDecisions: Moved back to England with family — explicit lifestyle choice over remaining in the SV epicentre.
Stopped operating; focused on writing long-form essays ('How To Do Great Work', 'Founder Mode').
Refused to start a fund or take a board seat — kept influence high, obligations low.
lessons: After accumulating power and wealth, the long-tail value is in the writing, not in another operating role.
Influence without obligation is the rare end state — most successful operators trade their freedom for one more title.
careerSteps.notes: Continues writing influential essays on paulgraham.com.

exitEvents.notes: Viaweb → Yahoo! Paid in Yahoo stock near dot-com peak values; PG held some through the crash but exit was effectively priced at this level.

outcomes.currentStatus: Investor, essayist, cultural architect of the startup world. Y Combinator has incubated companies whose aggregate valuation is reported above $600B.

lessons.lesson: Best founders are determined and flexible.
lessons.source: What We Look For in Founders

lessons.lesson: Wide exploration in your 20s compounds — don't optimise too early.
lessons.source: How to Lose Time and Money and others

lessons.lesson: Live in the right city — ambition is contagious.
Schlep blindness: the most valuable startup ideas hide in unglamorous problems.
Only have a startup if it is growing weekly — high-growth is the definition, not a feature.
Millionaire is achievable by hard work (Viaweb); billionaire requires some luck (Y Combinator).
Choose tools for leverage, not for the hiring market — small teams with sharp tools beat large teams with conventional ones.
Bet on people, not theses — the only way to be antifragile to your own being wrong about markets.

notes: Older-era role model — pre-AI tech revolution. Viaweb (1995) was a web-era startup and YC (2005) was a mobile/cloud-era institution; tactical specifics (Lisp as competitive edge, paying $0 office in Cambridge, batch model when nothing batched) DO NOT pattern-match cleanly to the AI era and should be treated as era-locked. His structural lessons (write to build audience and clarity; broaden in your 20s; found later than you think; choose tools for leverage; bet on people not theses) translate strongly. Weight: HIGH for principles, MODERATE for tactical timing. Education years for the painting phase overlap and are approximate from 'What I Worked On'.

researchLinks.hint: Godfather of startups. Excellent philosophy on making something people want. No get rich quick hacks- just doing work that benefits people, and ideally can be made to scale to lots (high growth startup - only have a startup if it is growing weekly). Advocates for young exploration (college, avenues) to develop as a person before startups (although amid AI may be naive- need to explore but be ready to pounce on an idea if it becomes clear- focusing on following the problems rather than the get rich quick hopes). Can get millionaire with hard work (viaweb), billionaire takes some luck (Y-Combinator).

firstCompany.name: Viaweb
firstCompany.oneLiner: Effectively the first online-store builder of its kind — a web app for non-technical merchants. Written in Common Lisp; acquired by Yahoo! in 1998 for ~$49M (became Yahoo! Store).
